title: The last confession
hook: a short prayer of confession said near death

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was visiting lightens: Akiva at the bedside of a student nobody else came to see. Who did you call or visit? Today we stay at the bedside, for the hardest conversation there is. Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

How do you tell someone who is very sick that it might be time to make their peace, without telling them they're dying? Jewish tradition has a sentence ready for exactly that moment, and it's a strange, kind one. Before the words of confession, the visitor says something like this: many have confessed and not died, and many have not confessed and died. In other words, saying this prayer is not a verdict. It doesn't summon anything. It's simply good to be ready. Today's word is the prayer that sentence opens the door to.
screen: `THE HARDEST CONVERSATION.` → `CONFESSING IS NOT A VERDICT.` → `IT'S GOOD TO BE READY.`

segments.voice: Vidui. Confession. The same word names the confession said on Yom Kippur, when a whole congregation admits its wrongs together. This one is said alone, or with a few people close by, near the end of life. Turn it four ways. First, the old instinct. The Talmud teaches that when a person falls ill and is close to death, they are told: confess. It's not a punishment. The Mishnah teaches that whoever confesses has a share in the world to come. Confession is a door, not a sentence. Second, the gentleness. The codes say not to raise it in front of people who will break down crying, so the sick person isn't frightened. If they can't speak, they can confess in their heart. If they can't manage the full text, a few words are enough. The tradition bends toward the person in the bed. Third, what it says. Wordings vary, but the short vidui acknowledges that healing and death are both in God's hands, asks for healing if it can be, asks that if death comes, it be counted as atonement for wrongs done, and asks for care for the family left behind. It is honest about both outcomes at once. Fourth, how it ends. Traditionally, the last words are the Shema: hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. The same line from childhood bedtime becomes the last line of all. Vidui is not about fear. It's about not leaving the important things unsaid. Ready.
screen: `THEY TELL HIM: CONFESS.` · `GENTLE, NEVER FRIGHTENING.` · `HONEST ABOUT BOTH OUTCOMES.` · `IT ENDS WITH THE SHEMA.` · then, large: `READY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about being ready. Nothing morbid. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself one quiet question: if today were my last, what would I wish I'd said? Let one thing come. An apology owed. A thank-you never sent. I love you, said out loud to someone who rarely hears it. Breathe with it. Then ask: is there any reason not to say it this week? Let your breath slow. If you pray, you can say the Shema slowly, or sit in silence. The bell holds the time.
Vidui. Confession: said near the end of life, gently, honest about healing and death, and closing with the Shema. Today's word.
Your line: ready. Today, say the one thing you'd hate to leave unsaid, or write it down where you'll find it. Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: When a Jew is gravely ill, a family member, friend or rabbi may gently offer to say the vidui with them, a short confession found in prayer books; it is often followed by the Shema.

fork.setup: your friend is very sick and wants to say vidui. relatives at the bedside are close to tears. what does the tradition advise?
options: say it loudly so everyone can join.
raise it gently, and not in front of those who will break down.
wait until the person can no longer hear.
fork.reveal: the codes say not to raise it before people who will weep, so the sick person isn't frightened; gentleness comes first.

original.note: Hebrew: confession, the same word used on Yom Kippur.

trapdoor: what you thought: a deathbed confession is about fear of punishment.
what it means: a gentle prayer, honest about healing and death, so nothing important is left unsaid.
what a scholar hears: Shabbat 32a's 'confess', and the Shulchan Aruch's reassuring line before it.
recall: a second yes, after bar or bat mitzvah

notes: Shabbat 32a ('when one falls ill... they tell him: confess') paraphrased; confirm.
Shulchan Aruch YD 338 (the reassuring line 'many confessed and did not die...', not before those who will weep, confess in the heart if unable to speak) paraphrased; confirm.
Content of the short vidui (healing and death in God's hands; atonement; care for family) described, not quoted; wordings vary. Confirm summary.
The Shema is rendered in plain English ('hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one'), not as a quotation; confirm acceptable.
Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:2 ('all who confess have a share in the world to come') paraphrased; confirm.
Editor: review no longer says Akiva swept the floor (Nedarim 40a has it swept before the student); now 'Akiva at the bedside of a student nobody else came to see'.
